tagline.text: On Maundy Thursday and Good Friday, carrozas with sacred images fill the streets

location.label: Location
location.text: Bantayan town, Bantayan Island, Cebu (the streets around Sts. Peter and Paul Parish Church)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Holy Week (March–April each year; around March 25–26 in 2027)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000–10,000 (1–2 nights in peak season, including lodging, boat and local transport)

children.text: Bantayan Island's Holy Week procession is a Catholic tradition in which carrozas (floats) carrying life-size sacred images pass through town on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday. Old island families have looked after the carrozas for generations to reenact the Passion of Christ, and the Santo Entierro (the burial of Christ) and Our Lady of Sorrows at the end of the Good Friday procession are the biggest sights.

The Holy Week (Semana Santa) procession on Bantayan Island, off northern Cebu, is a Catholic observance held every year on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday. Carrozas (floats) carrying life-size images fill the streets as they pass, showing the Passion and the Stations of the Cross in turn. It is a tradition that goes back a long way, and the island, usually known as a beach getaway, fills with people who come for the religious event. This entry is about an event, not a fixed attraction, so keep in mind that dates and schedules change every year.

The procession centers on Sts. Peter and Paul Parish Church in Bantayan town. According to Wikipedia, construction of the present church began in 1839 and took about 24 years; it is the fifth building on the site and is made of coral cut and dressed like stone. Earlier churches are said to have been burned during Moro raids, and a small museum inside is open by appointment. The town around this church is the stage for the procession, while the neighboring town of Santa Fe is better known for beaches and festivities, so many of the faithful cross over to Bantayan town for Lenten activities. In the 2024 census, Bantayan town had 87,394 residents, making it the largest and most populous town on the island, and it borders Madridejos to the north, Medellin to the east and Santa Fe to the south. The same source says the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul, called Palawod, is held on June 29 and Sinulog at the end of January, so festivals continue beyond Holy Week.

According to news reports, the procession is held twice, on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday, and in earlier years about 20 carrozas took part in each. The carrozas and images are passed down through the island's old families, who prepare them, and there is reportedly a formal handover to the family that will take charge the next year. A 2022 report says the event resumed with about 10 carrozas. The number can vary from year to year, so check this year's schedule with the parish and the town hall. How long the procession has lasted can be seen from the stories of it carrying on through disaster. Reports say that when a big fire struck the island during Holy Week in 1973, the procession continued even through the charred streets, and that after Super Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) in 2013 the people got back on their feet and prepared for Holy Week again. The event, which had been paused during the pandemic, returned in 2022.

Bantayan is also known as a place where eating meat is allowed during Holy Week. One story traces this to a papal indult from the 1840s, and the document is said to be kept in the parish museum, but its origin is not clear. This period is also peak tourist season for the island because the sea is calm and the holiday is long, and the media have voiced concern that the crowds are diluting the solemnity of Holy Week. When you watch the procession, show respect for it as a religious observance. Holy Week is also a holiday when most shops and offices close, so the whole island takes on the air of a family reunion.

A 2009 newspaper column says the procession starts with the largest carroza, the Last Supper (the twelve apostles and Jesus), followed by the Agony in the Garden, Judas's betrayal and the arrest, Jesus before Pilate, the scourging at the pillar and the crowning with thorns. The Escario family's carroza shows Jesus falling for the first time.

It begins with Peter's denial (the crowing rooster), followed by the stripping of Jesus, the nailing to the cross, the spear of Longinus and the descent from the cross. Carrozas belonging to the Hubahib–Yap family, the Pestaño family and the Mabugat family (the Pietà) are mentioned.

This carroza carries the body of Jesus in near-silvery white and is counted as the most awaited scene of the procession. The image is said to be more than a century old, and the whole procession is sometimes called the Santo Entierro (burial of Christ) procession.
At the very end of the procession come the carrozas of Our Lady of Sorrows (Mater Dolorosa) and Mary Magdalene, and the largest crowd follows them.

blocks.title: Families who carry on the tradition

children.text: Old families prepare the carrozas and images generation after generation, and Holy Week doubles as a family reunion. This system of family sponsorship of each carroza is what makes the event distinctive.
Children join the procession dressed as St. Peter, Our Lady of Carmel, the Archangel Michael or in angel wings. It is said that parents offer their children to God.
News reports say families come by motorized bangka from nearby islands, live aboard their boats and take part in the procession. Botigues and Doong islands are mentioned.
Sts. Peter and Paul Parish Church, in the town where the procession takes place, is an old church built of coral stone. A small museum inside is said to be open to visitors by appointment.

items.title: Two-day Holy Week plan
items.subtitle: Following the Maundy Thursday and Good Friday processions

children.text: Travel from Cebu City to a port in the north and take a boat to Bantayan Island. Boats are crowded during Holy Week, so leave early.
Check your lodging and look for a spot to watch the procession near the church in the town center. Check the parish and town hall announcements for the exact procession times.
Watch the Maundy Thursday procession and see the carrozas of the Last Supper, Gethsemane and Pilate in turn.
Find a place along the street before the Good Friday procession begins. The carrozas and the crowds fill the width of the street, so watch from a safe spot.
Watch the final part of the procession, when the carrozas of the Santo Entierro and Our Lady of Sorrows pass by. After the procession ends, leave quietly.
Relax at the beaches on the Santa Fe side, or book a visit to the museum in town, then head back.

I could not confirm the exact procession times and route because sources differ. Go by the latest announcements from the town hall and the parish. A 2009 column also tells how a sudden five-minute downpour fell after the Good Friday procession and was received as a blessing; outdoor processions can see changes in weather, so a rain jacket is a good idea.
Fly direct from Manila to Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB). Flight schedules change by season and Holy Week is very busy, so book early.
Bantayan Island is about
136 km
from Cebu City. Travel overland to a port in northern Cebu and take a boat.
A 2009 newspaper article says two shipping companies ran boats from Hagnaya Port to Bantayan and that the boats could carry cars. Operators and schedules may have changed, so check.
After arriving on the island, a guide says you take a jeepney from the Santa Fe ferry pier to the town of Bantayan.
Boats fill up during Holy Week, so book a few days ahead.
On the island you get around by tricycle and jeepney. Roads are blocked during the procession, so it is easier to move on foot.

The procession is held on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday, just before Easter. Easter changes every year, so check the calendar; in 2027 Easter falls on March 28, so Maundy Thursday is March 25 and Good Friday is March 26.

Holy Week is the busiest peak season on Bantayan Island because the sea is calm and the holiday is long. You need to book lodging and boats early, and if you want a quiet beach break it is quieter to avoid Holy Week.

During Holy Week the lodgings in Bantayan town and Santa Fe are nearly full, so reserve weeks ahead. To get a spot for the procession, a hotel in town close to the church is convenient, and if you prefer the beach you can stay in Santa Fe and travel by jeepney.

Bantayan is known as a place where meat is allowed during Holy Week, but restaurant hours may vary. Local home cooking and seafood are the basics. The island is known for egg and chicken production, enough to earn the nickname "egg basket of Cebu."

Bantayan town is a small town with old houses clustered around its central plaza. Typhoon Yolanda brought down two del Rosario houses on the plaza, and the D.C. Abello Theater was demolished in early 2015, so many old buildings have been lost. Before or after the procession, simply strolling around the plaza and the church gives you a feel for the island.
Check the latest announcements from the parish and the town hall for procession times and routes, which change every year.
The scenes differ between Maundy Thursday and Good Friday, so if you see both days the story fits together.
The carrozas are large enough to fill the width of the street and the crowd presses in, so look after your belongings and children.
The procession is a religious observance. Avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts, and do not get in the way of the carrozas or the faithful.
Take photos without flash, and do not point your camera at images or worshippers without permission.
There is little shade in the dry season, so bring a hat, water and sunscreen.
Lodging and boats fill up weeks before Holy Week, so book early.
Bring plenty of cash. The line at the ATM can be long in peak season.
Before watching the procession, take a look at the parish museum (by appointment) and the coral-stone church to better understand the story. Ask in advance whether you can visit.

Knowing the names of the families that look after the carrozas (Escario, Hubahib–Yap, Pestaño, Mabugat and others) makes the procession far more interesting. Local residents will sometimes share the stories handed down through generations.
The procession is one of the most solemn observances of the Catholic faith. Take part with respect, as part of worship, not as a spectacle.
The schedule, the number of carrozas and the route change every year, and the information in this entry is based on news reports and Wikipedia, so I could not confirm times.
In 2017 a local priest and the archbishop objected to a music festival planned for Holy Week. Entertainment events during Holy Week may be restricted or controversial.
Crowds are large, so watch out for pickpockets and congestion.
Many businesses may close or cut their hours during Holy Week, so check meals and transport in advance.
Even outside typhoon season, boats can be cancelled when the sea is rough, so leave some slack in your return plan.
The order of the carrozas in the 2009 column reflects that year. This year's order and number may differ, so follow the instructions on site.
Bantayan Island
is a resort island of beaches and fishing villages, a good place to relax at the beach after the procession.
Bantayan town
, the stage of the procession, is where the coral-stone church and the shops of the town center are found.
Santa Fe
is the neighboring town with beaches and the ferry pier, which serves as the island's entrance.
Daanbantayan
is a town in northern mainland Cebu close to Bantayan Island, on the way to Malapascua.
